name: Password Attacks & Cracking
tagline: Recover and test credentials you are authorized to attack: offline GPU/CPU hash cracking, hash identification, wordlists and rules, VPN PSK recovery, and lab-only NTLM relay, pass-the-hash and LSASS dumping chains.

tools.name: Hashcat
tools.desc: World's fastest password recovery utility: GPU-optimized OpenCL/CUDA kernels for 590+ hash modes across dictionary (-a 0), mask (-a 3), hybrid (-a 6/7), PCFG and rule-based (-a 0 -r) attacks, with a slow-hash tuning engine for salted/costed formats.
tools.when: The default for offline hashes you hold (dumps, configs, SAM/NTDS extract): benchmark, run wordlist + rules, then mask; benchmark against your own GPUs before buying cloud time.

tools.name: hashcat-utils
tools.desc: MIT-licensed stdin/stdout pipeline utilities (cap2hccapx, combipow, len, cutb, rulegen…) that pre-process captures and wordlists into exactly the candidate and hash formats hashcat expects.
tools.when: Convert WPA captures or normalize custom wordlists before a hashcat run; the companion tools to a serious cracking pipeline.

tools.name: John the Ripper
tools.desc: The classic Unix password cracker with dictionary, incremental (Markov), and rule modes; runs on CPU out of the box, and on OpenCL/hosted hardware in jumbo builds.
tools.when: First port of call for /etc/shadow-style hashes and any environment without working GPU drivers; pairs with your own .conf rules.

tools.name: John the Ripper jumbo
tools.desc: Community 'bleeding-jumbo' branch adding hundreds of extra hash/cipher formats (NTLM, macOS, PDF, RAR, KeePass, FortiGate, IKE-PSK) plus the *2john converters used to package encrypted files before cracking.
tools.when: Whenever your hash or file format is not covered by stock John or hashcat — the widest offline-format coverage available.

tools.name: Hashtopolis
tools.desc: Self-hosted client/server platform that distributes hashcat workloads across many GPUs on your own fleet, with task queues, chunking, and a web UI for assigning hash lists and attack modes.
tools.when: Fill a lab or rented cloud-GPU rack with crack work: a Hashtopolis server dishes out chunks to each agent and consolidates results for your authorized recovery jobs.

tools.name: GoCrack
tools.desc: FireEye's manager/worker framework written in Go for managing password-cracking tasks across a cluster of GPU hashcat workers, with a web panel for task packaging and result retrieval.
tools.when: An alternative to Hashtopolis when you want a Go-native manager for a reclaimed GPU cluster; archived but still runnable for lab workflows.

tools.name: hcxtools
tools.desc: Converts Wi-Fi captures (pcapng) and probe/eapol frames into the PMKID and PBKDF2 hashes that hashcat and John crack directly — the modern replacement for binary service packs.
tools.when: Process a 4-way-handshake or PMKID capture from your own access point on the way to an offline WPA2/WPA3 Purge PSK attack.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ZerBea/hcxtools && make && sudo make install

tools.name: aircrack-ng
tools.desc: The de-facto Wi-Fi suite: airodump-ng for capture, aireplay-ng for handshake injection, and aircrack-ng for dictionary/PTW attacks against WEP and WPA/WPA2 across your own networks.
tools.when: Authorized wireless testing of infrastructure you operate: capture the handshake, verify the client, then hand the hash to hashcat for the heavy lifting.

tools.name: hashid
tools.desc: Python regex identifier for 220+ hash types that prints the matching hashcat mode (-m) and John format, so the correct cracking command is chosen before the first run.
tools.when: The moment you collect a hash (dump, config, CTF): identify it before picking -m/--format to avoid wrong-mode and line-length failures.

tools.name: Name-That-Hash
tools.desc: Friendly command-line and web-identifying hash analyst that recognizes her way through common formats and prints the matching hashcat and John modes with sample hashes.
tools.when: A zero-friction second opinion on ambiguous hashes (e.g. distinguishing NTLM from MD4/NDSS) before you commit to a cracker.

tools.name: hashes.com sample hashes
tools.desc: Online database documenting sample hashes and lookup methods for a wide range of algorithms (MD5, NTLM, bcrypt, Argon2, Joomla, …) useful for confirming a suspect format.
tools.when: Cross-check an unusual hash against documented samples, or eyeball expected lengths/salt formats before choosing an engine.

tools.name: Hashcat example hashes
tools.desc: Official table with one valid sample hash per hashcat mode (password is always 'hashcat'), including VPN PSK (5300/5400/2500) and firewall (7000) formats; also embedded via hashcat --example-hashes.
tools.when: Confirm your hash formatting and attack command offline before a live run, or label unknown samples in your own CTFs.

tools.name: SecLists
tools.desc: The security tester's companion collection: passwords (10k/1M/rockyou-derived), usernames, default router credentials, and discovery/fuzzing payloads in one tree.
tools.when: First stop in any authorized recovery or login test — reach for its dictionaries before generating anything custom.

tools.name: rockyou.txt
tools.desc: The 2009 RockYou leak (~14M real-world passwords) that remains the standard baseline dictionary for fast-hash testing; shipped with Kali and mirrored in SecLists.
tools.when: Quick first-pass dictionary sweep against fast hashes you own before rule/mask work, exactly as Kali documents it.

tools.name: OneRuleToRuleThemAll
tools.desc: Community-curated single hashcat .rule file merging the best of popular rule sets (NSAKEY, d3ad0ne, etc.) so one base wordlist yields high-coverage candidate mutations.
tools.when: A proven default ruleset for the dictionary+rule phase (-a 0 -r) when you don't want to hand-tune your own .rule file.

tools.name: hashcat best64.rule
tools.desc: The stock best64.rule ships in the hashcat repo and applies 64 high-yield mangles (append digit, toggle case, leetspeak, suffix) — the quickest low-cost rule win.
tools.when: A fast, predictable ruleset that is safe to run on the default pool before heavier custom rules.

tools.name: Openwall John rules
tools.desc: John's rule engine and wiki-documented preset rules (dumb, wordlist, KoreLogic, single) mutate base words with case, suffix, prefix and substitution pipelines.
tools.when: Applying John-side rule sets in jumbo-supported formats, especially when you are already cracking with john rather than hashcat.

tools.name: Pipal
tools.desc: Wordlist statistics analyzer that reports password length, character set, repeated digits, baseword frequency and pattern bias so you can shape the right attack.
tools.when: Analyze your own leaked/test wordlist before building rules: learn the shape (e.g. 'capitalized word + 2 digits') and pick efficient masks.

tools.name: statsprocessor
tools.desc: Hashcat's position-based password generator that derives per-position character frequencies from a wordlist and emits statistically weighted masks for -a 3 attacks.
tools.when: Turning observations from your wordlist scans into a frequency-driven mask attack that outperforms naive charsets.

tools.name: Mentalist
tools.desc: Graphical wordlist builder centered on human password paradigms: case mangling, keyboard walks, year/digit insertion, exporting full lists or ready-made hashcat/John rules.
tools.when: Visually profile a candidate password space (vocab + year + symbol) when you prefer a GUI over hand-editing rule files.

tools.name: kwprocessor
tools.desc: Hashcat-team keyboard-walk generator producing passwords that follow adjacent-key routes and basechars/config surprises for PINs and passphrases typed on keyboards.
tools.when: Target PINs and passphrases your own devices generate along keyboard patterns, where walk-derived guesses beat pure randomization.

tools.name: crunch
tools.desc: Character-set wordlist generator enumerating all combinations/permutations with @,%^ pattern placeholders plus output splitting, resume and gzip/7z output.
tools.when: Generate bounded, pattern-shaped candidate lists (known prefixes/suffixes, specific charsets) to feed hashcat or John.

tools.name: CeWL
tools.desc: Ruby spider that crawls a site to a depth and emits the unique words (plus author/email metadata) it finds — a vocabulary completely specific to that target.
tools.when: Build organization-specific dictionaries (your own web app, a CTF) where site vocabulary beats generic lists.

tools.name: CrackStation
tools.desc: Free online hash cracker (MD5, SHA1, NTLM, and 220+ other algorithms) that matches your hashcat modes against massive precomputed tables.
tools.when: A quick single-hash sanity lookup during analysis; treat as a confirmation aid, never as your primary recovery path for sensitive data.

tools.name: Kerbrute
tools.desc: Go-based userenum/passwordspray tool that walks Kerberos pre-authentication: it discovers valid users from KDC error codes and tests one password against many accounts without lockouts.
tools.when: Authorized domain testing where you need lockout-safe spraying via AS-REP pre-auth and user enumeration against your own KDC.
tools.install: Download release binary from the repo, or go install github.com/ropnop/kerbrute@latest

tools.name: NetExec
tools.desc: The fork-lifted successor to CrackMapExec; its kerberos module performs password spraying and user enumeration across your SMB/Kerberos estate with clean protocol handling.
tools.when: Office-wide spray validation when you already carry a NetExec install and want one client for SMB, LDAP, Kerberos and SSH checks.

tools.name: Spray
tools.desc: Small Python sprayer that takes a forged inventory of usernames and a handful of passwords, sleeps between attempts, and reports hits plus failed-auth stats.
tools.when: Lockout-conscious spraying against your own AD from a Linux attack box with randomized delays.

tools.name: TREVORspray
tools.desc: Python sprayer against Microsoft 365/Azure AD and AD with strong anti-lockout controls (seasonable delays, account randomization, MFA-threshold guardrails).
tools.when: Azure AD/Office 365 authorized spray testing where you must respect MFA lockout and per-account backoff.

tools.name: DomainPasswordSpray
tools.desc: The canonical community PowerShell sprayer: enumerates domain users from AD, tests one password across them, detects lockdown policies and can pass an existing password.
tools.when: Classic AD password-spray validation in your own estate with built-in user enumeration and graceful exit on failure.

tools.name: MSOLSpray
tools.desc: Python sprayer for Azure Active Directory / Microsoft 365: validates tenant, tests credentials via MSOL endpoints and reports valid user texture plus lockout status.
tools.when: Authorize-and-run check of Azure AD accounts in your own tenant without tripping global lockout thresholds.

tools.name: o365spray
tools.desc: Username enumeration and password spraying against Microsoft 365 / Azure AD with built-in rate limiting, module-based spraying and user check against MSOL open endpoints.
tools.when: Coverage of M365 as the primary cloud sprayer when you need mature lockout-safe logic built in.

tools.name: sprayshed
tools.desc: Lockout-aware password-spray / brute-force orchestrator against localhost lab services; dry-run by default so nothing is touched without confirmation.
tools.when: Staged, lockout-safe credential testing against services you own (lab only).

tools.name: Responder
tools.desc: LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS poisoner in a lab: it answers name-resolution queries and captures NTLMv1/v2 challenge-response hashes from clients that voluntarily submit them.
tools.when: Lab/pentest only: run it to demonstrate why your own network filters these protocols, and feed captured that to a relay or cracker.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/lgandx/Responder && cd Responder && sudo proxychains4 -i tcp -v python3 responder.py -I eth0

tools.name: mitm6
tools.desc: IPv6 abuser for labs: advertises a rogue DHCPv6 server so Windows clients register DNS and hand over WPAD traffic that can feed NTLM credential relaying.
tools.when: Building a relaying pipeline against your own IPv6-enabled lab where clients trust rogue DHCPv6 — pair with ntlmrelayx, lab only.

tools.name: impacket ntlmrelayx
tools.desc: The relay half of the chain: accepts captured NTLM authentications and replays them to SMB/LDAP on targets you control, enabling hash history recording or relayed logins without knowing the plaintext password.
tools.when: The canonical lab relay server after a poisoning daemon harvests NTLM; keep every target in your own lab scope.
tools.install: pip install impacket; python3 ntlmrelayx.py -t smb://<lab-target>

tools.name: impacket psexec / wmiexec
tools.desc: Impacket's psexec and wmiexec use an NTLM hash directly to open an administrative service/exec on a Windows host — no password needed, lab authors' flagship use case for hash validation.
tools.when: After you hold a hash for a machine in-scope: psexec for a service-metered shell, wmiexec for a cleaner WMI-backed execution.

tools.name: NetExec (pass-the-hash)
tools.desc: Netexec smb/winrm handles pass-the-hash logins (-H) at scale, checks admin rights and executes commands — replacing CrackMapExec workflows with an active fork.
tools.when: Sweep several lab hosts with one hash to map who accepts admin hash logins; identical protocol coverage keeps it a natural psexec alternative.
tools.install: pipx install netexec; nxc smb 127.0.0.1 -u admin -H :NTHASH

tools.name: evil-winrm
tools.desc: WinRM shell client that authenticates with a password or NTLM hash and gives an interactive PowerShell session for post-hash validation.
tools.when: Clean, HTTP-bound lab session when WinRM is open and you prefer a stable PowerShell interactive to service-write tricks.

tools.name: Mimikatz
tools.desc: The lab-standard post-exploitation credential extractor: reads LSASS memory to dump plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets and DPAPI keys on systems you administer.
tools.when: Authorized lab/engagement 'logonpasswords' runs on endpoints you own to prove how cached secrets age; always on-lab, never stealth marginal.
tools.install: Download release from the repo and run sekurlsa::logonpasswords on your own host

tools.name: lsassy
tools.desc: Python library that grabs and parses LSASS memory via WMI/remote scripts without landing a binary on the target, returning parsed credentials for lab review.
tools.when: Remote-to-itself lab extraction on Windows endpoints you operate, minimizing artefact noise compared to writing a standalone dump.

tools.name: DonPAPI
tools.desc: DPAPI-centric credential dumper that walks LSASS and protected-store databases plus DPAPI master keys on remote machines, carving secrets and their derivation chains.
tools.when: Lab DPAPI-focused extraction where you want the credential chain laid out and don't need a full interactive shell.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/login-securite/DonPAPI && pip install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: firepwd
tools.desc: Pure-Python decryptor for Mozilla Firefox/Thunderbird logins.json driven by the derived master-password key; recovers saved site credentials from a copy you own.
tools.when: Inspect the saved logins of your own Firefox profile (e.g. a forgotten master password) on a copy, never someone else's browser data.

tools.name: SharpDPAPI
tools.desc: C# DPAPI toolkit from the GhostPack family that decrypts Chrome/Edge vaults, DPAPI master keys and credential files on Windows — the standard for authorized browser-store recovery.
tools.when: Recover Chrome/Edge saved credentials on machines you administer, using your own user context/master key.
tools.install: Download the compiled release or build from source, run from your own session

tools.name: LaZagne
tools.desc: Python credential-store dumper that walks browsers, WiFi profiles, mail clients, SSH keys and many desktop apps, recovering stored logins and passwords from your own machine.
tools.when: One-shot sweep of every local credential store on a system you own for DR/hygiene or lab inventory.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/AlessandroZ/LaZagne && cd LaZagne && python3 laZagne.py all

tools.name: hashcat VPN PSK modes (IKE-PSK 5300/5400, Cisco-IPSEC 2500)
tools.desc: Dedicated hashcat modes crack IKE pre-shared keys (5300/5400) and Cisco IPSEC VPN hashes (2500/500) captured from phase-1 handshakes, alongside FortiGate (7000) formats for firewall admin hashes.
tools.when: Recover a PSK for a VPN you administer when the key was mis-remembered; pair with ike-scan for the phase-1 capture first.

tools.name: ike-scan
tools.desc: IKE discovery and testing tool that sends phase-1 negotiation to a VPN gateway and captures the responder's hash — the handshake you feed straight into hashcat's IKE-PSK modes.
tools.when: Grab a legitimate IKE PSK exchange from a VPN endpoint you own, then crack it offline with hashcat for key-hygiene validation.

tools.name: John *2john archive converters
tools.desc: zip2john, rar2john and 7z2john turn encrypted ZIP/RAR/7z archives into $zip$/$rar$/$7z$ hashes that john jumbo or hashcat crack by password.
tools.when: Recover a forgotten password on your own archive: convert once, then crack with john -jumbo or hashcat after wordlist+rule passes.

tools.name: fcrackzip
tools.desc: Fast zip password cracker with dictionary and brute-force modes (libzip-based fork runs far faster than the unzip-spawning original).
tools.when: A quick direct brute/dictionary check of a small single ZIP without standing up a John pipeline; superseded by *2john for real workloads.

tools.name: pdf2john
tools.desc: John/jumbo converter that extracts the hash from password-protected PDFs (RC4 and AES variants) and feeds it to john or hashcat for offline recovery.
tools.when: Open a PDF you own whose password was lost: convert to the $pdf$ format and crack on your own CPU/GPU.

tools.name: keepass2john
tools.desc: John jumbo converter that packages a sealed .kdbx KeePass vault into a $keepass$ hash crackable by John or hashcat, covering the current PBKDF2 runtime cost.
tools.when: Unlock your own KeePass vault after the master password drifted; always work on the copy you own, never a database you don't control.

tools.name: pdfcrack
tools.desc: Dedicated GPL tool recovering owner/user passwords from PDFs using the classic security handler (rev 2-4) via wordlist or brute force with state save/restore.
tools.when: Recover legacy (pre-AES-256 rev 5) PDFs you own; on modern AES R4/R6 documents prefer pdf2john's formats instead.
